scenes.text: Every time you send a message to a chatbot, someone pays for it. [1] Sometimes a fraction of a rupee, sometimes much more. [2] So where does the cost of AI actually come from? Let's break it down.

There are two big costs. [1] Training, a huge one time cost, to build the model. For the biggest models, it can be hundreds of millions of dollars. [2] Inference, a small cost every time someone uses it. Tiny per message, but it adds up with millions of users.

left.title: Training
left.label: huge cost to build the model

scenes.text: [1] APIs charge per token, from episode 3. [2] Input tokens, the text you send, including documents and chat history. [3] Output tokens, the text the model writes, which usually cost several times more. [4] Longer conversations cost more, because the history is sent again, every turn.

data.definition: AI APIs charge by the number of tokens read and written. Output tokens usually cost more than input.

scenes.text: Here's what drives the bill. [1] Model size, bigger models cost more per token. [2] Prompt length, long documents and chat history. [3] Answer length, long answers cost more. [4] Number of calls, agents may call the model many times, for one task. [5] And traffic, multiplied by every user.

So how do teams cut costs? [1] Use the smallest model that does the job well. [2] Keep prompts short, and send only relevant chunks, with RAG. [3] And use caching, reusing answers, and repeated prompt parts, instead of paying again.

Here are four terms. [1] Price per million tokens, how APIs list their prices. [2] Prompt caching, a discount when the start of your prompt repeats. [3] Batch processing, cheaper prices if you can wait for results. [4] And latency, how long you wait, which often trades off against cost.

Here's a common myth. [1] People think free chatbots cost nothing to run. [2] Every answer uses GPUs and electricity. Free plans are paid for by subscriptions, investors, or limits on how much you can use.

data.myth: Free chatbots cost nothing to run.
data.fact: Every answer uses GPUs and electricity. Free plans are paid for by subscriptions, investors or usage limits.
